Bokkie the Turtle

By: Diana Lucas | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
21st October 2023, South Africa is on on high after their nail biting win 16 -15 against England.
Not 12 hours later barnacle covered turtle is washed up on Struisbaai beach. She’s rescued by a local and contacts Leon Volke, one of the many volunteers up and down South Africa’s coastline. These volunteers make up The Turtle Rescue Network.

The Two Oceans Aquarium in Cape Town is where she ends up. Here its also a nail biting couple of days for the aquarium team to see if this barely alive turtle - covered with green algae and barnacles and an amputated front flipper- will survive.

Its touch and go but she does and does and is named “Bokkie” in honour of our South African Springboks. This is Bokkies story from her rescue, to her rehabilitation to her soon to be release. Her story will be told by the various people who have been in her life, on land. From the Leon at the rescue; the vet, Bernice; Talitha, who runs the turtle rehab at the aquarium / Aleysha volunteer to the team who release her.


Further information:
Once Bokkie had been cleaned and placed in a freshwater bath to help her rehydrate, Bernice the vet, decided on a treatment plan. Over the first two months of her being in Critical Care at the Turtle Conservation Centre, she received pain therapy, antibiotics, wound treatment, and regular freshwater baths.
She is the first patient at the Turtle Conservation Centre to receive total parenteral nutrition (TPN) treatment. This means Bernice injected a mixture of nutritional supplements into Bokkie’s blood system. The team chose this method as Bokkie was refusing to eat any food, so TPN was the best option to ensure that she continued to receive nutrients and sustenance.
You may think that Bokkie’s biggest problem was her amputated front flipper… Well, think again. Three days after she arrived at the Turtle Conservation Centre, she pooped out a large piece of plastic. Five days after that, she pooped another three pieces of plastic. There was a short break in the excretion of plastic, until mid-November when she pooped out dozens of pieces of plastic in quick succession.
Bokkie is a record-breaker at the Turtle Conservation Centre: She has excreted over 47 pieces of plastic.
Bokkie's reluctance to eat in the first few weeks at the Turtle Conservation Centre was due to gut stasis. This is when the gut shuts down and everything within the gut becomes hard. In Bokkie's case, the gut stasis was even more severe due to the presence of all the plastic she had consumed.
Thankfully, the 47th piece of plastic was Bokkie’s last piece. At the end of November, she had started eating and was healthy enough to be moved from the Critical Care area to the main rehabilitation centre. Today she can be seen swimming around the largets tank in the aquarium and has developed a strong following.! Her amputated flipper doesn’t hinder her as much as you’d think – she still has an elbow joint that helps her with mobility.
Plastic is one of the biggest problems polluting the water and the turtles mistake them for jelly fish. Tracy manages the Turtle Rescue network, which is made up of over 1000 volunteers along the Western Cape Coastline. Her rescue Diary records every rescue
For years the Turtle Conservation Centre has been doing what they can with limited resources facing and ever-increasing problem because of discarded fishing nets, boat accidents and other hazards. But now the main cause is the plastic pollution in our seas. The increasing number of injured and stranded turtles can no longer be accommodated on the Aquarium roof and so in April the announcement of a one-of-a-kind Turtle Conservation Centre to be built at Granger Bay is being made.

The new Centre will be open to the public and have state-of-the-art veterinary science facilities. It hopes to support turtle rehab on the entire African continent. Aside from its conservation importance the Centre will also be a major educational and tourist attraction.

“We hope these beautiful animals will act as Ambassadors in reminding us to care for our Oceans.”
Bokkie’s rehabilitation journey thus far is a testimony to the resilience of these incredible animals. From being rescued on the beach in a rough state and passing a shocking 47 pieces of plastic to being a healthy turtle with a strong appetite and an even stronger future
In early May, Bokkie will be released a very emotional moment for the team, and we will be there.

Script:


Link
He’s nailed it….its over……it’s simply unbelievable…there it is…there it is the Springboks Hands aloft…. The Bokke have done it….
The morning after South Africa’s nail biting win at the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi finals a green turtle was washed up on Struisbaai beach,
Talitha: It was a tight game I cant remember the details we got called out because this turtle had arrived, and she had this injury and we needed to respond to it but we were all feeling incredibly patriotic and so she was going to be our Bokkie.
VO
Adult and subadult turtles, like Bokkie, strand on the Western Cape coast throughout the year. Their two biggest threats fishing nets and plastic ingestion
Talitha: The reason they wash up is because they have got nothing left inside them.
V/O
You could call Talitha Nioble-Trull , ‘Guardian of the Turtles’ She’s head of the Turtle programme at Two Ocean’s Aquarium Foundation.
TALITHA NOBLE-TRULL
CONSERVATION MANAGER
TWO OCEANS AQUARIUM FOUNDATION
We have an incredible rescue network there is a tribe of turtle rescuers on the WC coastline so as soon as someone finds a turtle the network is activated do then its like Aaa I can drive from Struis Baai to the N2, some one else can drive them from N2 to peregrine farm stall and then you get this action.
V/O
And within a few hours Bokkie was on Dr Bernice Van Huyssteen’s examination table, at the Turtle Conservation Centre, part of Cape Town’s Two Oceans Aquarium,
DR BERNICE VAN HUYSTEEN
SEA TURTLE VETERINARIAN
TWO OCEANS AQUARIUM FOUNDATION
When she came in they took off almost a kilogram of barnacles from her bottom side thats how long she had been sick and drifting she had things growing on her,* She was dehydrated, she was weak she wasn’t eating. So she was in a pretty debilitated state.
V/O
Bokkie was found missing a front flipper, and it looked like this amputation had happened a while ago… but that was not her biggest problem… she had eaten plastic, and a lot of it.
Just 3 days after she arrived, she excreted 47 different pieces of plastic.
Bernice: I think that was the most plastic we have had passed in one of these turtles…one was a full size money bag that came through intact and so It was incredible that she could survive and get through all of that.
Talitha
If you think about a green turtle in the wild they are eating jellyfish, they are eating algae, grass growing and a lot of plastic she had consumed looked very similar to those things.
UP Sound: ‘I think she likes this, you reckon…pretty soothing’
V/O
It took a month of treatment in Critical Care…pain relief, antibiotics, nutritional supplements injected directly into her bloodstream before Bokkie’s condition was stable, and she was let loose in the big tank.
Mac She’s also become a bit of a celebrity right?
Talitha: Turtles have this ability to hold 2 things at the same time this incredible, very sobering reality which is our impact on them – the 47 pieces of plastic that she should not have consumed and simultaneously hold this hope. You look at Bokkies eyes, you see her moving her stump and you just can't help but fall in love with her and so the two together are very powerful. It means that Bokkie and turtles like her have this ability to be ambassadors to make you want to love and protect their home.
Alex: Bokkie’s been a little fighter from the beginning and she’s very inquisitive, very sweet but she can also be spicy.
V/O
Once Bokkie had healed the goal was to get her release ready And that’s the role of Turtle behaviourist Alex Panagiotou,

ALEX PANAGIOTOU
SENIOR AQUARIST
TWO OCEANS AQUARIUM FOUNDATION

Alex
You can tell the ones that want to fight harder than others and she was one of those. Very motivated, very A + student. So the kind of enrichment we did with her was mostly physical because other than that cognitively she was bright.
Talitha I think three flipper turtles are a different type of turtle. They have got something to prove. So ja, when we look at Bokkie we see a very determined brave and strong turtle…Much like the Springboks actually.
Mac: A bit of resilience right?
Talitha …we call it turtle tetrus when we figure out who needs to go in which pool
V/O
The turtle conservation centre is tightly squeezed onto the roof of the aquarium… and while there are plans for an upgraded facility, in the meantime they make do with what they have. And thankfully Bokkie and Luna - a turtle who's been at the centre since February - are ready to move out.

Talitha It’s a great indicator that they are release ready when they start to behave like kids who have had too much sugar in a confined space. She is now looking for trouble, she needs to be going home.
Link
So there’s Bokkie with her little amputated flipper and this is where her journey is going to begin from here she gets releases into the wild and hopefully lives the rest of her turtle life in the ocean
V/O
The day before her release, Bokkie is lured into the smaller tank and hoisted up for a final medical check up.
Mac touches her skin….its soft!!!
Mac: How has her weight changed from the time she arrived to where she is right now?
Bernice: She has become nice and chubby* she’s done very well.
V/O
Before Bokkie’s re entry into the ocean, she is fitted with a satellite tag. Turtles as endangered species are vulnerable, the tag will give us a valuable glimpse into her world.
Taitha: We put a lot of effort into caring for these turtles, it’s a hospital, they have come to us on the brink of death. We put all love and care into them and then we put them back where they belong out in the ocean we don’t know, what her journey holds and tracking turtles allows us to answer some of those questions.
V/O
It’s been a year since Bokkie’s rescue. Early on the 20th October she and her co rehab turtle Luna are taken out of the water and wrapped up like newborn’s.
V/O
Surprisingly the release will be not in the Cape waters but at Isimangaliso Wetland Park in KwaZulu Natal..
Talitha
Our weather in CCT is not suitable for release at the moment. The ocean is wild and stormy and cold but she is ready and she needs to go home so the next option is to fly her to somewhere more suitable. The beauty of Isimangaliso is twofold. It is a protected space so you can release these turtles there knowing there is a little bit of a buffer before you have got all these other threats that they are going to encounter.
V/O
It takes great organisational skill and manoeuvring to keep the release operation on track. The team’s priority is to keep the turtles’ stress levels to a minimum
Mac: For suuch long periods being outside the water will that not impact them in any way?
Alex: They can be out of water for a very long time because they air breathing so that’s great. The main worry is dehydration. So we will be putting some water based lubricant on them that will keep the moisture inside. We will put eyedrops in their eyes and then keep them at a nice temperature so they don’t get cold, or overheat.
Mac: So tell us about the release, where in Cape Town we have got to get to Durban somehow what is that going to be like?
Alex: It's going to be interesting. It’s going to be the first time for all of us doing this method, we are going to fly commercial.
Mac: So they are not going to be in little boxes underneath the plane ?
Alex: They are going to be with us ya
Mac: Getting Chicken or beef?
Alex: Exactly or fish, for that reason other than the stretcher you saw today we have created a little carrier for them so they feel a bit more protected and also so they don’t mess the plane
V/O
From King Shaka International Airport, the South African Association for Marine Biological Research assists with the last leg of the journey, transporting the turtles four hours away to Isimangaliso Wetland.
Talitha: This is a really exciting big day, we are going to release turtles here today . We've got 12 loggerhead hatchlings and two green turtles
Alex
The scariest part is we don't have control over what's out there and mostly due to threats it can be a scary place so I think it’;s important for all of us to play our role to make the ocean a safer place so when we do release them there is nothing for us to fear.
V/O
Luna’s first …..Bokkie awaits her fate,
Up sound : Mac Whoa he’s trying to come out..
…a whiff of the ocean air must stir memories
V/O
And with a little help from her friends… - space turtle Bokkie – With her Satellite tag – goes in….
Link
It's so beautiful to see Bokkie finally getting into the water, you can't help being emotional about it and wishing her all the best.

Promo 1

Talitha: This is a really exciting big day, we’re going to release some turtles here today

V/O
One year after she was rescued, from the brink of death, Bokkie, a green turtle goes back to the ocean.

Alex …..as soon as she smelt the ocean she couldn’t wait to go back…she crawled she got into the water and she was off.



Promo 2
A green turtle, covered in algae and barnacles and missing a flipper is found stranded on the beach.

Talitha
The reason they wash up is because they have got nothing left inside them

Link 142
It was touch and go but the turtle survived

Alex
Bokkie has been a little fighter form the beginning

V/O
Now Bokkie is ready to back to the ocean

Promo 3
Mac touches her skin….its soft!!!
V/O
It’s been a year since Bokkie, a green turtle, was found stranded on the beach, she’s now ready for new adventures.
Talitha It’s a great indicator that they are release ready when they start to behave like kids who have had too much sugar in a confined space. She is now looking for trouble, she needs to be going home.

Alex: They can be out of water for a very long time because they air breathing so that’s great. The main worry is dehydration. So we will be putting some water based lubricant on them that will keep the moisture inside. We will put eyedrops in their eyes and then keep them at a nice temperature so they don’t get cold, or overheat. Mac: So tell us about the release, where in Cape Town we have got to get to Durban somehow what is that going to be like? Alex: It's going to be interesting. It’s going to be the first time for all of us doing this method, we are going to fly commercial. Mac: So they are not going to be in little boxes underneath the plane ? Alex: They are going to be with us ya Mac: Getting Chicken or beef? Alex: Exactly or fish, for that reason other than the stretcher you saw today we have created a little carrier for them so they feel a bit more protected and also so they don’t mess the plane V/O From King Shaka International Airport, the South African Association for Marine Biological Research assists with the last leg of the journey, transporting the turtles four hours away to Isimangaliso Wetland. Talitha: This is a really exciting big day, we are going to release turtles here today . We've got 12 loggerhead hatchlings and two green turtles Alex The scariest part is we don't have control over what's out there and mostly due to threats it can be a scary place so I think it’;s important for all of us to play our role to make the ocean a safer place so when we do release them there is nothing for us to fear. V/O Luna’s first …..Bokkie awaits her fate, Up sound : Mac Whoa he’s trying to come out.. …a whiff of the ocean air must stir memories V/O And with a little help from her friends… - space turtle Bokkie – With her Satellite tag – goes in…. Link It's so beautiful to see Bokkie finally getting into the water, you can't help being emotional about it and wishing her all the best. Promo 1 Talitha: This is a really exciting big day, we’re going to release some turtles here today V/O One year after she was rescued, from the brink of death, Bokkie, a green turtle goes back to the ocean. Alex …..as soon as she smelt the ocean she couldn’t wait to go back…she crawled she got into the water and she was off. Promo 2 A green turtle, covered in algae and barnacles and missing a flipper is found stranded on the beach. Talitha The reason they wash up is because they have got nothing left inside them Link 142 It was touch and go but the turtle survived Alex Bokkie has been a little fighter form the beginning V/O Now Bokkie is ready to back to the ocean Promo 3 Mac touches her skin….its soft!!! V/O It’s been a year since Bokkie, a green turtle, was found stranded on the beach, she’s now ready for new adventures. Talitha It’s a great indicator that they are release ready when they start to behave like kids who have had too much sugar in a confined space. She is now looking for trouble, she needs to be going home.

metadata.Summary: 21st October 2023, South Africa is on on high after their nail biting win 16 -15 against England. Not 12 hours later barnacle covered turtle is washed up on Struisbaai beach. She’s rescued by a local and contacts Leon Volke, one of the many volunteers up and down South Africa’s coastline. These volunteers make up The Turtle Rescue Network. The Two Oceans Aquarium in Cape Town is where she ends up. Here its also a nail biting couple of days for the aquarium team to see if this barely alive turtle - covered with green algae and barnacles and an amputated front flipper- will survive. Its touch and go but she does and does and is named “Bokkie” in honour of our South African Springboks. This is Bokkies story from her rescue, to her rehabilitation to her soon to be release. Her story will be told by the various people who have been in her life, on land. From the Leon at the rescue; the vet, Bernice; Talitha, who runs the turtle rehab at the aquarium / Aleysha volunteer to the team who release her.
metadata.Further information: Once Bokkie had been cleaned and placed in a freshwater bath to help her rehydrate, Bernice the vet, decided on a treatment plan. Over the first two months of her being in Critical Care at the Turtle Conservation Centre, she received pain therapy, antibiotics, wound treatment, and regular freshwater baths. She is the first patient at the Turtle Conservation Centre to receive total parenteral nutrition (TPN) treatment. This means Bernice injected a mixture of nutritional supplements into Bokkie’s blood system. The team chose this method as Bokkie was refusing to eat any food, so TPN was the best option to ensure that she continued to receive nutrients and sustenance. You may think that Bokkie’s biggest problem was her amputated front flipper… Well, think again. Three days after she arrived at the Turtle Conservation Centre, she pooped out a large piece of plastic. Five days after that, she pooped another three pieces of plastic. There was a short break in the excretion of plastic, until mid-November when she pooped out dozens of pieces of plastic in quick succession. Bokkie is a record-breaker at the Turtle Conservation Centre: She has excreted over 47 pieces of plastic. Bokkie's reluctance to eat in the first few weeks at the Turtle Conservation Centre was due to gut stasis. This is when the gut shuts down and everything within the gut becomes hard. In Bokkie's case, the gut stasis was even more severe due to the presence of all the plastic she had consumed. Thankfully, the 47th piece of plastic was Bokkie’s last piece. At the end of November, she had started eating and was healthy enough to be moved from the Critical Care area to the main rehabilitation centre. Today she can be seen swimming around the largets tank in the aquarium and has developed a strong following.! Her amputated flipper doesn’t hinder her as much as you’d think – she still has an elbow joint that helps her with mobility. Plastic is one of the biggest problems polluting the water and the turtles mistake them for jelly fish. Tracy manages the Turtle Rescue network, which is made up of over 1000 volunteers along the Western Cape Coastline. Her rescue Diary records every rescue For years the Turtle Conservation Centre has been doing what they can with limited resources facing and ever-increasing problem because of discarded fishing nets, boat accidents and other hazards. But now the main cause is the plastic pollution in our seas. The increasing number of injured and stranded turtles can no longer be accommodated on the Aquarium roof and so in April the announcement of a one-of-a-kind Turtle Conservation Centre to be built at Granger Bay is being made. The new Centre will be open to the public and have state-of-the-art veterinary science facilities. It hopes to support turtle rehab on the entire African continent. Aside from its conservation importance the Centre will also be a major educational and tourist attraction. “We hope these beautiful animals will act as Ambassadors in reminding us to care for our Oceans.” Bokkie’s rehabilitation journey thus far is a testimony to the resilience of these incredible animals. From being rescued on the beach in a rough state and passing a shocking 47 pieces of plastic to being a healthy turtle with a strong appetite and an even stronger future In early May, Bokkie will be released a very emotional moment for the team, and we will be there.
